passage:
Tuesday night, 11:40

Swati asked me at lunch why I'm always so tired if I got the job everyone wanted. I laughed it off. I shouldn't have. It's a good salary. My parents tell everyone. But today I spent eight hours making slides nobody will read, and the only good hour was when I helped the new intern understand the system. She said, "You explain so clearly!" and I felt more awake than all week.

Is that stupid? Wanting to teach when I finally have money?

I'm not quitting tomorrow. I have loans. But I want to notice what makes me feel like that again. Maybe I'll volunteer to train new joiners. Maybe I'll ask Swati how she chose. She seems happy.

Going to sleep. 😴
— Manoj

qa.q: What was the only good hour of Manoj's workday?
qa.a: It was the hour spent helping the new intern understand the system.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling while writing 'Is that stupid?'
qa.a: Manoj felt unsure and a bit guilty for wanting something other than the well-paid job Manoj's parents are proud of.

qa.q: What small step does Manoj plan that fits Manoj's situation?
qa.a: Manoj plans to volunteer to train new joiners and talk to Swati, exploring what brings energy without quitting yet.

qa.q: How might Swati see Manoj's tiredness?
qa.a: She noticed it and asked, which suggests she senses Manoj is not happy despite the good job.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing that meaning at work may come from something other than salary and status.

passage:
Sabina: can I tell you something weird
Rajni: always
Sabina: I got the bank offer. the big one
Rajni: WHAT congrats!! 🎉
Sabina: and I feel nothing
Rajni: nothing?
Sabina: like I should be jumping. everyone at home is
Sabina: but the one thing I loved this year was the weekend library project with the kids
Rajni: you literally glowed talking about that
Sabina: ammi says that's a hobby, not a life
Rajni: maybe it can be both? or maybe it's a clue
Sabina: I don't know what to do with a clue
Rajni: you don't have to decide tonight
Rajni: maybe talk to people doing work like that. see what their days are really like
Sabina: ok. yeah. thanks for not just saying congrats
Rajni: 🤍

qa.q: What project did Sabina love this year?
qa.a: Sabina loved the weekend library project with the kids.

qa.q: Why does Sabina feel 'nothing' about the bank offer?
qa.a: The job brings status and pride at home, but it doesn't connect to what actually made Sabina feel alive this year.

qa.q: What sensible next step does Rajni suggest?
qa.a: Talking to people doing that kind of work to learn what their days are really like, without rushing a decision.

qa.q: How might Sabina's mother see the situation differently?
qa.a: She sees the library project as a hobby and the bank job as security, so she may worry about Sabina giving up a stable path.

grounding: Shows a young adult questioning whether a high-status job is enough and exploring what gives life meaning.

passage: Pooja finished her engineering degree and came home to Nashik district for the summer, expected to take the city job her uncle had arranged. Instead she kept ending up at the village school where her old teacher, Chandrika-bai, still taught. The roof leaked, and the science cupboard was empty. Pooja began bringing old bottles, magnets and batteries, and the children crowded around her. One evening Chandrika-bai asked, "What do you want your days to feel like, not your salary?" Pooja didn't have an answer. She walked home past the fields, turning the question over. She still planned to take the city job. But she wrote down the days she'd felt most herself, and nearly all of them were at that school.

qa.q: What did Pooja bring to the village school?
qa.a: She brought old bottles, magnets and batteries.

qa.q: What does Pooja's lack of an answer to Chandrika-bai suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had never really asked herself that question and was unsure what she truly wanted.

qa.q: What was wise about how Pooja responded to the question?
qa.a: She didn't make a sudden decision but started noting the days she felt most herself, gathering clues about meaning.

qa.q: How might the schoolchildren see Pooja's visits?
qa.a: They likely see her as exciting and generous, someone who makes science feel real in a school with an empty cupboard. 😊

grounding: Shows a young graduate starting to explore what makes work worthwhile beyond a secure, arranged job.

passage: Aiko had two envelopes on the desk of her small Sendai apartment. One held an offer from a large trading company in Tokyo, the salary printed clearly, the kind of job her parents could mention to the neighbours. The other was a note from the community centre where she had volunteered for three years, asking if she would run their after-school reading programme, for far less money. She walked along the river with Yuki, her friend from university. 'Which days from last year do you actually remember?' Yuki asked. Aiko didn't have to think: the afternoon a shy boy read a whole page aloud, and the old librarian clapping. Not one of her internship days came to mind. 'That doesn't decide it,' Aiko said. 'Money matters too.' But she wrote both lists that night, and the second one was much longer.

qa.q: Where had Aiko volunteered for three years?
qa.a: At the community centre.

qa.q: What does Aiko's 'Money matters too' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She was genuinely torn; the memories pulled her towards meaningful work, but she did not want to dismiss practical needs.

qa.q: How did Yuki's question help Aiko?
qa.a: Asking which days she remembered pointed her to what felt worthwhile, adding meaning to a decision that had been about salary and status.

qa.q: How might Aiko's parents see her choice?
qa.a: They might prefer the Tokyo job they could proudly mention, and find the community centre role hard to understand at first.

grounding: Shows a graduate abroad weighing a prestigious salary against work that feels worthwhile to her.

passage: The night shift at the district hospital in Bhubaneswar was quiet until two, when an old man in bed six began calling for his wife. Bidisha, a second-year nursing student, sat with him, holding his hand until he fell asleep. At the tea counter Lakshmi, the senior nurse, asked why she had chosen nursing. 'Honestly? Papa said it was a safe job, and I could go abroad later.' Bidisha stirred her tea. 'I used to count the months till I could leave. Tonight I didn't think about money once.' Lakshmi nodded. 'That feeling won't come every shift. Some nights are just charts and tiredness.' 'I know,' Bidisha said. 'But now I know it exists.' She wrote the time and bed number in her pocket diary, not for the chart, but for herself.

qa.q: Which bed was the old man in?
qa.a: Bed six.

qa.q: What change in Bidisha's feelings does her comment about money reveal?
qa.a: Sitting with the patient gave her a sense of worth beyond the safe-job reason she had started with.

qa.q: Why is Lakshmi's reply useful for Bidisha?
qa.a: She is honest that this feeling will not come every shift, helping Bidisha hold on to purpose without expecting every night to feel special.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for the old man?
qa.a: Frightening and lonely until someone held his hand, which let him settle and sleep 🤍

grounding: Shows a nursing student discovering meaning in her work beyond salary and security during a night shift.

passage:
Dear Chetan,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Here's the honest version. The job is good. The salary is more than Papa earned at fifty. I have a desk by the window and free lunch. And by Wednesday every week I feel like a photocopy of myself.
Two Saturdays ago I went with my flatmate to teach maths at the community centre near the railway colony. A girl called Pinky finally understood fractions by folding a roti into quarters, and she shouted so loudly the others clapped. I walked home more awake than I've felt in three months of work.
I'm not quitting. I'm not that brave, and home needs the money. But I've asked my manager about the company's volunteering days, and I'm going every Saturday. Maybe meaning isn't one big choice. Maybe it's where you keep showing up.
Write back. Tell me what makes your weeks feel real.
Eshaan

qa.q: How did Pinky finally understand fractions?
qa.a: By folding a roti into quarters.

qa.q: What does Eshaan mean by feeling like a photocopy by Wednesday?
qa.a: Eshaan feels empty and flat at work, despite the good salary and comforts.

qa.q: What realistic step did Eshaan choose, and why does it fit the situation?
qa.a: Asking about volunteering days and teaching every Saturday, which adds meaning without giving up the income home needs.

qa.q: How might Chetan respond to the question at the end?
qa.a: Chetan would likely feel trusted by the honesty and might start thinking about what makes his own weeks feel real.

grounding: A young employee writes to a friend about finding meaning beyond a good salary through regular volunteering.

passage: Dolma, pour the tea and don't laugh. Remember how I, Jasleen, planned my whole life at nineteen? Big company, big city, a car by twenty-five. I got the internship. Gurgaon, glass tower, my own ID card on a ribbon. And I felt nothing. Not sad, just flat, like the air-conditioning got into my chest. Then last monsoon, during the floods, I came home to Ropar and helped the gurdwara volunteers pack food for three days straight. My back hurt, I slept four hours a night, and I was happier than I'd been all year. So now I ask myself one silly question every night: what would I do on a Tuesday if nobody was watching? The answer keeps coming back: something with my hands, with people, where I can see the difference. I don't know the job yet. Maybe public health. Maybe relief work. But I'm done choosing by the car.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen do the internship?
qa.a: In Gurgaon, in a glass tower.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling at the internship?
qa.a: Jasleen felt flat and empty, not exactly sad, despite reaching the planned goal.

qa.q: How is Jasleen's nightly question useful for finding direction?
qa.a: Asking what to do on a Tuesday with nobody watching separates real values from status, pointing to hands-on work with people.

qa.q: How might Dolma react to Jasleen's change of plan?
qa.a: Dolma might be surprised, remembering the car plan, but probably glad to hear Jasleen sound so sure.

grounding: A young adult tells a friend how flood relief work showed that purpose matters more than status.

passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and I sat next to Ujjwal in the placement hall in Aizawl the day both his offers came through. One was a bank: good salary, a title his parents could tell relatives about. The other was a school counsellor's post in Lunglei, paying about half. I watched him read the bank letter twice and put it face down. He read the school one and kept his thumb on it, as if keeping his place. He didn't say anything for a long time. At lunch he told me his younger brother had struggled at school and nobody noticed until it was almost too late. That was all he said. A week later he told me he had taken the Lunglei post. His father didn't speak to him for three days. I don't know if he was sure. He looked tired. But when he left for Lunglei, he was smiling on the bus.

qa.q: Where was the school counsellor's post?
qa.a: In Lunglei.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have been feeling as he kept his thumb on the school letter?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed drawn to it, perhaps torn and nervous, as if his brother's story made the counsellor's post feel worthwhile.

qa.q: What could help someone in Ujjwal's place weigh two offers like these?
qa.a: Thinking about which work would feel worthwhile, as the brother's story did for Ujjwal, and talking openly with family about the reasons.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's father have felt about the choice?
qa.a: His father was probably disappointed and worried about the lower pay and status, which may be why he stayed silent for three days.

grounding: A classmate watches a young man choose a lower-paid counselling post over a bank job for the sake of meaning.

passage:
Before: In January, Chandrika started a high-paying job at a consulting firm. She had a big salary, a nice flat, and a strange emptiness every Sunday night.
During: In April, her friend Hemant took her to his weekend volunteering at a children's library in a basti. She read stories to kids who had never held new books. She came home tired but lighter than she'd felt in months.
She went back every weekend. She asked herself: what would I do if salary didn't matter?
After: In October, she didn't quit, but she moved to the firm's education practice, and still spends Saturdays at the library. The salary is a little less. Sunday nights are different now.

qa.q: Where did Hemant volunteer at weekends?
qa.a: At a children's library in a basti.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling on Sunday nights in January?
qa.a: Chandrika felt empty and restless despite her good salary.

qa.q: What steps helped Chandrika find more meaning?
qa.a: Volunteering regularly, asking what she'd do if salary didn't matter, and moving to work closer to her values.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel seeing Chandrika's change?
qa.a: Hemant probably feels happy and proud he invited her.

grounding: Over months a young woman explores meaning beyond salary and shifts her work direction.

passage:
Amandeep, you asked me whether to take the bank job or the teaching job. Let me tell you about my choice.
When I was twenty-two, I got two offers: a government office job with good security, and a job teaching science in a village school for less money.
Everyone told me to take the office job. I did, for a year. I was comfortable and bored. I kept thinking about the village kids I'd met during my internship.
One day, I asked myself: when I'm old, what will I be glad I did? I resigned and went to the school.
It was hard. Less money, more work. But forty years later, I still get letters from students. Your Sahil nana says: think about what you'll be glad of, not just what's safe.

qa.q: What job did young Sahil take first?
qa.a: A government office job.

qa.q: What was young Sahil feeling in the office job?
qa.a: Sahil felt comfortable but bored and unfulfilled.

qa.q: What choice inside the story changed Sahil's life direction?
qa.a: Asking what Sahil would be glad of when old, then resigning to teach in the village school.

qa.q: How might Sahil's students have felt about his choice?
qa.a: Sahil's students were likely grateful, which is why they still write to him.

grounding: A grandfather tells how he chose meaningful work over a safe job.

passage:
Kavitha had twenty-four hours to accept a job at a big tech company. The salary was double what she earned at the small non-profit where she worked on water projects.
She called her friend Lalit at midnight. "I can't decide."
"What do you love about your current job?"
"When a village gets clean water, I feel like my work matters."
"And the tech job?"
"Money. Status. My parents would be thrilled."
"Could you do meaningful work there?"
"Maybe. But not the kind I care about."
Kavitha slept badly. In the morning, she declined the offer, then called her parents to explain. Her father was quiet. Then he said, "If it makes you happy, beta."

qa.q: How many hours did Kavitha have to accept the tech job?
qa.a: Twenty-four hours.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she called Lalit at midnight?
qa.a: Kavitha felt torn and anxious about the decision.

qa.q: What question from Lalit helped Kavitha decide?
qa.a: Asking what she loves about her current job helped her see her sense of purpose.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's father feel about the decision?
qa.a: Her father might be disappointed but accepts it because he wants her to be happy.

grounding: Under time pressure a young woman chooses meaningful work over a higher salary.

passage:
Kishore had the job everyone in his Mumbai colony wanted: software, good salary, air-conditioned office. At twenty-two, he bought his parents a new fridge. But on Sunday evenings he felt a dread he couldn't explain.
His school friend Akash taught maths to kids from the nearby basti on Saturdays, in a community hall. He dragged Kishore along once. "Just help with the laptops."
Kishore ended up spending two hours with a girl named Pinky who wanted to make a game. When she got a character to jump, she screamed so loudly the whole hall turned.
Kishore walked home feeling something he hadn't felt at the office in months. He didn't quit his job. But he went back the next Saturday, and the next. On Sunday evenings, the dread was quieter. Salary paid the bills. Saturdays made the week worth something.

qa.q: What did Pinky want to make?
qa.a: A game.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling on Sunday evenings before the Saturdays?
qa.a: Kishore felt a dread he couldn't explain, despite his successful job.

qa.q: What does Kishore's story suggest about finding meaning?
qa.a: Meaning can come from something outside salary and status, like helping someone learn, and it doesn't always require quitting a job.

qa.q: How might Akash see Kishore coming back every Saturday?
qa.a: Akash probably feels glad and a bit proud that his friend found something that matters to him.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult exploring what makes life worthwhile beyond salary and status.

passage:
"Why are you awake?" Naveen asked, finding Deepika on the terrace at 2 a.m.
"Thinking. I got the bank job offer."
"That's great!"
"Is it? Good money. Safe. Everyone's proud. But I keep thinking, is this it? Forty years of spreadsheets?"
Naveen sat down. "What would make it worth it?"
"I don't know. When I volunteered at the animal shelter, I didn't check the time once."
"So maybe it's not the job. Maybe it's what else you do. Or maybe later you build something at the bank that helps people."
"Or maybe I'm just scared."
"Could be all three."
Deepika laughed. "You're useless."
"I'm honest. Take the job. Keep the shelter. Keep asking the question."
She looked at the city lights. "Keep asking the question. Okay."

qa.q: Where had Deepika volunteered?
qa.a: At the animal shelter.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling about the bank job offer?
qa.a: Deepika felt uncertain and a little scared, unsure whether safety and pride were enough to make life worthwhile.

qa.q: What did Naveen suggest, and why is it realistic?
qa.a: Take the job, keep volunteering and keep asking what matters, because purpose can grow over time rather than being decided in one night.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel sitting with a friend at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Naveen probably feels caring and patient, glad to help Deepika think without pushing an answer.

grounding: Shows through dialogue a young adult questioning whether salary and status are enough and exploring purpose.

passage:
In my final year, my parents expected me to take the job at the bank where my father worked. I'm Sabina, and I had the offer letter in my bag for two weeks without signing it.
My friend Rashmi asked me one night, "When did you last feel like the day mattered?" I told her about the month I'd spent helping at a rural health camp: carrying files, calming scared patients, translating for a doctor. I'd been exhausted and completely awake.
I didn't suddenly quit everything. I talked to Abbu first. He was hurt, then quiet, then he asked, "Would you regret not trying?" I said yes.
So I applied for a public-health master's. I got in. The stipend is small. Some days I miss the idea of the easy life. But when I'm at a camp, I don't check the time.

qa.q: How long did Sabina keep the offer letter without signing?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel during the month at the health camp?
qa.a: Sabina felt exhausted but completely awake, as if the days mattered.

qa.q: What helped Sabina decide, and what could others learn?
qa.a: Rashmi's question and an honest talk with Abbu helped; asking when life felt meaningful can guide choices beyond salary and status.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when Sabina chose the master's?
qa.a: Abbu was probably hurt at first, then accepting and quietly proud that Sabina chose with care.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing a path based on meaning rather than salary and family expectation.

passage:
Counsellor's note, final-year guidance sessions (Irfan, careers cell)
Kamal came in for the third time this month. On paper his situation is simple: a placement offer from a large firm, a good salary, his parents delighted. Yet he says he feels "nothing" when he thinks about it. Today he talked for twenty minutes about the weekend maths classes he runs for children in his neighbourhood, and his voice changed; he leaned forward, laughed, remembered every child's name. I did not tell him what to choose. I asked him to list three moments this year when he felt useful, and three when he felt only busy. He came back in ten minutes. All three useful moments involved teaching. Next step: he will talk to two teachers about their actual working days before deciding anything, and keep the offer open while he does.

qa.q: What does Kamal run on weekends?
qa.a: He runs maths classes for children in his neighbourhood.

qa.q: What does the change in Kamal's voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels genuinely excited and alive about teaching, in contrast to the flat "nothing" he feels about the offer.

qa.q: Why was Irfan's approach helpful?
qa.a: Instead of choosing for Kamal, Irfan used a simple list and suggested talking to real teachers, so Kamal can find a direction with facts 🙂

qa.q: How might Kamal's parents see his hesitation about the offer?
qa.a: They are delighted with the offer, so they might feel confused or worried that he is doubting a good job.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young adult exploring what makes work worthwhile beyond salary and status.
